newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMAN RELIEF ON EU TINGED WITH CONCERN ABOUT FRANCE.
newsitem.headline: GERMAN RELIEF ON EU TINGED WITH CONCERN ABOUT FRANCE.

text.p: Germany's relief at the European Union summit's support for a stability pact for its single currency was tinged on Tuesday with concern that the past week's differences with France over the euro would not be the last.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel were tactfully upbeat after the Amsterdam summit backed the strict pact, leaving it to the popular Bild daily to put it in black and white in a headline reading "Germans get their way!"

Business leaders like Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), were ready to accept a French-sponsored jobs chapter in the revised Maastricht treaty because it would, as he said, "be without any great effect".

But the strains of the past week, after France's new Socialist-led government said it could not accept the stability pact as it stood, left their traces in the brooding comments made in some of Germany's leading newspapers.
"The fundamental conflicts between French and German econonic and financial policy have not disappeared," Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung noted in an editorial.

"The French government demands more political influence over European monetary policy," it wrote. "But only an independent central bank modelled on the German Bundesbank can ensure a stable euro in the long term."
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung agreed: "The fundamental dissent between Germans and French over stability policy continues to smoulder."

The stability pact, the high price Germany demanded for giving up its deutschemark currency, requires members of European economic and monetary union (EMU) to pay stiff fines if they overshoot the Maastricht convergence criteria.

The pact, which tightens the EMU guidelines in the 1991 Maastricht treaty, is seen here as the best way to ensure that sceptical German voters accept the new currency and not rebel against Kohl in general elections next year.
The Westdeutsche Allgemeine said the dispute between Paris and Bonn over the stability pact was just a foretaste of what would come after the launch of the single currency.

"The arguments about monetary policy, about the sense of a stable currency and the way of handling state debts will continue. They will even become more intense when the currency union actually starts," it predicted.
"This is all the result of the fundamental weakness of the currency union -- that it is lacking the necessary political basis," it added.
Most commentators stressed that Germany and France, each other's closest partner and the core alliance driving European unity, could both present the deal as a success.
"But there is no reason for celebration," the Frankfurter Allgemeine wrote. "The solution is just like most Brussels compromises: it is too thin to have any durability.
"It helps the French to save face at home. But it will not be of much use either to them or their partners."
The Frankfurter Rundschau said the accord on coordinating job creation in Europe was -- like previous state attempts to boost employment -- "a paper tiger, regardless of what paper it is written on".
Bonn's General Anzeiger agreed with German politicians that the structural problems of inflexible labour markets could only be solved by national governments.

"Decisive is that the future single currency community decided on a stability pact that guarantees a strong euro. Otherwise employment problems would just have got worse -- despite any jobs pacts," it wrote. REUTER
